hints: Think about what stays the same in any type of isomerism and what is special about stereo, focus on arrangement in space rather than connectivity.
walkthrough:
Separate connectivity from geometry**
Picture two models built from the same kit with the same atoms joined in the same order. That is the same structural formula. Stereoisomers keep that connectivity identical, so no bonds are moved to different atoms.

Add the space idea**
Now imagine you keep all the connections fixed but twist one part into a different position in 3D space, like left hand versus right hand or cis versus trans around a double bond. That different spatial arrangement with the same connectivity is stereoisomerism.
Final answer: Molecules with the same structural formula but with a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space.

hints: Look closely at Fig. 6.1 for carbons with four different groups attached and for a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond with two different groups on each carbon.
Recall how each chiral centre doubles the number of optical isomers and how one cis-trans $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond doubles it again.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centres**
Look at the five membered ring in $\text{V}$. The two ring carbons that carry side chains each have four different groups attached, one H, one side chain, and two different ring directions. So you have 2 chiral centres. Each one can be R or S, which alone would give $2^2 = 4$ optical isomers.

Spot the geometrical unit**
Now look at the side chain $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Each $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ has two different groups and rotation is restricted, so cis and trans forms are possible. That is an extra factor of 2.

Combine the factors**
Think multiplicatively. 4 arrangements from the chiral centres multiplied by 2 arrangements from the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ gives $4 \times 2 = 8$ stereoisomers in total.

Final answer: Number of stereoisomers = 8
Reasoning: V has 2 chiral centres and 1 $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond that shows cis-trans (geometrical) isomerism, so $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.

hints: Count all carbons carefully including the ring (5), the ester side chain ($\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$) and the alkene side chain, then add hydrogens to give each carbon four bonds.
walkthrough:
Count carbons and oxygens from the skeleton**
Let me count with you. Ring gives 5 C. Left side $\text{-CH}_2\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{OCH}_3$ gives 3 C. Right side $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ gives 5 C. Total $5+3+5 = 13$ C. Oxygens are 2 in the ester plus 1 in the ring ketone, total 3 O.

Fill in hydrogens**
Each saturated $\text{CH}_2$ needs 2 H, each $\text{CH}$ needs 1 H, $\text{CH}_3$ needs 3 H, and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ or quaternary C needs 0 H. Adding them all gives 20 H, so $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}_{3}$.

hints: Scan Fig. 6.1 for the $\text{-CO}_2\text{CH}_3$ group, the ring $\text{C}=\text{O}$, and the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in the side chain.
walkthrough:
Label each oxygen containing group**
The $\text{-CH}_2\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{OCH}_3$ end is a classic ester, $\text{RCO}_2\text{R'}$. The $\text{C}=\text{O}$ inside the five membered ring with carbons on both sides is a ketone, not an aldehyde.

Add the hydrocarbon unsaturation**
The side chain contains $\text{CH}=\text{CH}$, a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, so the alkene functional group is also present.
Final answer: Ester and ketone (carbonyl) and alkene ($\text{C}=\text{C}$).

hints: Compare V with W in Fig. 6.2, note which bonds gain hydrogen, the ring $\text{C}=\text{O}$ becomes $\text{CH-OH}$ and the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{-CH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Track what changes from V to W**
Look side by side. The ring ketone $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in $\text{V}$ becomes $\text{CH(OH)}$ in $\text{W}$. That is gain of hydrogen. At the same time the side chain $\text{CH}=\text{CH}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$. That is also gain of hydrogen.

Name the role**
Gain of hydrogen, or loss of oxygen equivalent, is reduction. Because $\text{T}$ reduces two different functional groups, its role is a reducing agent for both $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and $\text{C}=\text{C}$. The ester is untouched, so $\text{T}$ is selective for those two groups.
Final answer: Reducing agent for both the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ (ketone) and the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ (alkene).

hints: Compare W with X, in reaction 2 the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ is retained while the ketone is still reduced to an alcohol, so think of a hydride reagent that reduces $\text{C}=\text{O}$ but not $\text{C}=\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
See the selectivity in reaction 2**
In $\text{X}$ the ring ketone has become an alcohol but the side chain $\text{CH}=\text{CH}$ is still there. So $\text{U}$ reduces $\text{C}=\text{O}$ but leaves $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and ester alone.

Recall the classic reagent**
That pattern is exactly what $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ does. It is a mild hydride donor that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but does not attack isolated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bonds or esters under normal conditions.
Final answer: Sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_{4}$.

hints: Recall that the small peak at $m/e = 201$ is due to one $^{13}\text{C}$ in a molecule containing only $^{12}\text{C}$ at $m/e = 200$, and that $\text{Q}$ has one carbon fewer than $\text{Y}$ because methanol is lost.
Use the relationship relative height $= n \times 1.1\%$, where $n$ is the number of carbons, with the $M^+$ peak set to 100.
walkthrough:
Work out n from the reaction**
$\text{Y}$ is like $\text{V}$ but with a saturated side chain, so it has 13 carbons. Fig. 6.3 shows $\text{Y} \rightarrow \text{Q} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. One carbon leaves as methanol, so $\text{Q}$ must contain $13 - 1 = 12$ carbons. Call this $n = 12$.

Link n to the M+1 peak**
The peak at $m/e = 200$ is $M^+$ with all $^{12}\text{C}$, height 100. The peak at $m/e = 201$ is molecules with one $^{13}\text{C}$. Natural abundance of $^{13}\text{C}$ is about $1.1\%$. So expected height is:
$$x = n \times 1.1 = 12 \times 1.1 = 13.2$$

Show the working as a ratio**
You can write it as $$\frac{100 \times x}{1.1 \times 100} = 12$$ which rearranges to $x = 13.2$. That matches a 12 carbon molecule.

Final answer: $n = 12$ carbons in $\text{Q}$
$$\frac{100 \times x}{1.1 \times 100} = 12$$
$x = 13.2$

hints: Recall what functional group gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and check whether Y still has its ketone while Q contains only hydroxyl groups.
walkthrough:
Remember what 2,4-DNPH detects**
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts only with carbonyls, aldehydes and ketones, to give an orange solid. Alcohols and esters or acids do nothing.

Apply to Y and Q**
$\text{Y}$ still has the ring ketone $\text{C}=\text{O}$, so it gives the orange precipitate. $\text{Q}$ is stated to contain only hydroxyl groups, so no carbonyl is present and no precipitate forms.
Final answer: Y: orange precipitate; Q: no precipitate (no reaction).

hints: Write the equation for $\text{ROH} + \text{Na}$ and note that 1 mol of $\text{OH}$ gives 0.5 mol of $\text{H}_2$.
Convert $44.8\text{ cm}^3$ of gas at s.t.p. to moles using $24000\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$ (or $22400\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$ as defined) and compare with $0.0020$ mol of $\text{Q}$.
walkthrough:
Write the key stoichiometry**
Each hydroxyl group reacts as:
$$\text{ROH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2}$$
So 1 mol $\text{OH}$ produces 0.5 mol $\text{H}_{2}$. If a molecule has two $\text{OH}$ groups it will produce 1 mol $\text{H}_{2}$ per mol of molecule.

Convert the gas volume to moles**
Moles of $\text{H}_{2}$ produced:
$$n(\text{H}_{2}) = \frac{44.8}{22400} = 0.0020\text{ mol}$$
You started with $0.0020$ mol of $\text{Q}$, so:
$$\frac{n(\text{H}_{2})}{n(\text{Q})} = \frac{0.0020}{0.0020} = 1$$
One $\text{H}_{2}$ per $\text{Q}$ means two $\text{OH}$ groups per $\text{Q}$, because each $\text{OH}$ gives half a $\text{H}_{2}$.

Final answer: $$\text{ROH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2}$$
Moles $\text{H}_{2} = 44.8 / 22400 = 0.0020$ mol from $0.0020$ mol $\text{Q}$, so ratio $\text{Q} : \text{H}_{2} = 1:1$, hence 2 $\text{OH}$ groups per molecule.

hints: Use Table 6.2 to find the wavenumber range for $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in a ketone or ester and think about which of Y or Q still contains it.
Use Table 6.2 to find the wavenumber range for hydroxy $\text{O-H}$ and think about which of Y or Q contains hydroxyl groups.
walkthrough:
Pick out the carbonyl difference**
$\text{Y}$ contains ketone and ester $\text{C}=\text{O}$ groups. Table 6.2 places $\text{C}=\text{O}$ at about $1670-1740\text{ cm}^{-1}$ (ester $1710-1750\text{ cm}^{-1}$). So $\text{Y}$ will have a strong peak or trough there. $\text{Q}$ has only hydroxyl groups, no $\text{C}=\text{O}$, so that absorption is absent.

Pick out the hydroxyl difference**
$\text{Q}$ contains alcohol $\text{O-H}$ groups. Table 6.2 places hydroxy $\text{O-H}$ at $3200-3650\text{ cm}^{-1}$ as a broad absorption. So $\text{Q}$ will show this band. $\text{Y}$ has no $\text{O-H}$, so it will not show it. Only the region above $1500\text{ cm}^{-1}$ is considered.

Final answer: Y shows absorption at $1670-1740\text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}=\text{O}$, Q does not.
Q shows broad absorption at $3200-3650\text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{O-H}$ (hydroxy), Y does not.
